articles.body:
One of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said she wants to avoid “circular arguments” about whether the UK should rejoin the EU, underlining divisions at the top of government over revisiting Brexit.

Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, appeared to suggest she was not in favour of rejoining the trade bloc, but she said the prime minister should still pursue closer ties to fulfil the promises made at the time of the referendum.

She is one of a handful of cabinet ministers who are concerned about Burnham’s plan for an “honest conversation” with the public about Brexit and who are privately warning it could reopen a row that would only benefit Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.

“I do not believe that anybody wants to repeat circular arguments about in or out, leave or remain. I do think, though, that over the last decade we have let the British people down very badly,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

Nandy, whose Wigan seat voted overwhelmingly for leave in 2016, and who is one of the most cautious in the cabinet about reversing Brexit, was asked if she wanted to go back in. “I don’t know if that’s a choice we have,” she said.

However, she did concede that Burnham was trying to address the failings of the Brexit deal, telling Sky News it was important to “be honest” and highlight that “the deal that we got is not what we were promised”.

The culture secretary stressed there were “trade-offs and choices” to be made which involved a conversation with people across the country, indicating that Brexit would be a key theme of the next election campaign.

Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday. Downing Street sources said he would use it to get Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.

In private, EU counterparts will be expecting Burnham to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to move beyond Labour’s “red lines” on the bloc after the next election.

At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and youth experience visas are expected to be confirmed.

Burnham said at the weekend there was more to come. “This summit will show what we can achieve when we work together, but it doesn’t need to be the end of our ambition,” he told the Sunday Mirror.

Officials will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €150bn (£125bn) Safe defence fund, collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and visas for touring artists.

Soon after the Brussels summit, Burnham is expected to give a speech setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU, arguing it would be in the UK’s long-term interest. No 10 sources said he wanted to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion.

Senior government figures say Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be solely confirmatory.

“You can’t ask people to vote on an undefined plan like in 2016. That was David Cameron’s mistake,” one said.

However, Burnham has faced reservations from others within his cabinet. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, are cautious about pushing to fully rejoin.

The EU’s former chief Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier said London could not have the “single market à la carte” by cherrypicking which of the four freedoms – including freedom of movement – it would like in future negotiations.

“There is no cherrypicking. There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other,” he told the BBC.

Nandy was forced to reject allegations that celebrating the UK rejoining the Erasmus plus scheme by linking it to Remembrance Sunday was inappropriate, after suggesting it would help to honour “the immense courage of those who served our country” before Remembrance Sunday.

Kevin Hollinrake, the Tory chair, suggested she was using the national civic occasion to “try to make an EU membership pitch”. He said: “Our veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme.”

Speaking on Sky News, Nandy responded: “They are the only party that is talking about Brexit and the EU. What we are announcing this weekend is that we’re going to widen the Erasmus scheme.

“I cannot see what is political about saying that we want young people from every part of this country to understand the contribution that their grandparents and great-grandparents made, not just to us but to many, many lives of people that they had never met,” she added.

articles.title: Eisenkot open to Netanyahu joining Israel’s next government
articles.summary: Israel's president officially tasks the opposition leader with forming a new government.
articles.preview: Israel’s president officially tasks the opposition leader with forming a new government. Israel’s opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, the man officially tasked by President Isaac Herzog with trying to form the country’s next government, has said that he was open to including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his coalition lineup. In a speech at Sunday’s ceremony in Herzog’s office in Jerusalem, Eisenkot suggested Netanyahu’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich was also welcome to join.
articles.body:
Israel’s president officially tasks the opposition leader with forming a new government.

Israel’s opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, the man officially tasked by President Isaac Herzog with trying to form the country’s next government, has said that he was open to including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his coalition lineup.

In a speech at Sunday’s ceremony in Herzog’s office in Jerusalem, Eisenkot suggested Netanyahu’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich was also welcome to join.

“If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented,” Eisenkot said.

Eisenkot, who ran as Netanyahu’s main rival, has six weeks to form a new government. At the ceremony, Eisenkot said he will act in the interests of the public and represent all parts of Israeli society.

Herzog, meanwhile, warned that the country faced uncertainties after the November 3 midterm elections in the United States, which brought victories for several political figures critical of Israel and the US’s military support.

“The State of Israel needs a stable government,” Herzog said, pointing to the “new political reality” in the US.

Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.

Despite this, Arab-led parties endorsed Eisenkot for the mandate to replace Netanyahu.

In Israel’s October 27 elections, Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats.

Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.

He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote.

“Netanyahu still has time to derail Gadi Eisenkot’s efforts to form a government and sabotage attempts to gain a vote of confidence,” said Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank.

“In the meantime, he remains caretaker prime minister. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would be the natural second in line to be tasked with forming a government. And if he fails, elections would then be called, and that would still allow Netanyahu to remain as caretaker.

“Many of Netanyahu’s critics say that is his aim. The big question in Israeli politics now is: does the opposition really want to get rid of Netanyahu? Or is the opposition to Palestinian Israelis in mainstream politics so strong that they’re willing to risk keeping Netanyahu in power by going back to the ballot box?”

articles.preview: Exclusive: Louise Haigh likely to weaken mandate for sales that forms key part of emission reduction plan Analysis: Climate always comes second – are green issues slipping down Burnham’s agenda? Ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government’s electric vehicle (EV) targets this week, in a move that will relieve carmakers but alarm many Labour MPs who are worried about the government’s commitment to the green agenda.
articles.body:
Ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government’s electric vehicle (EV) targets this week, in a move that will relieve carmakers but alarm many Labour MPs who are worried about the government’s commitment to the green agenda.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalise the plan after a crunch meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday to settle a long-running dispute between the transport, energy and business departments.

Haigh is expected to agree to cut a target for EV sales by about a quarter, government sources say, helping British industry but setting up a potential fight with MPs and campaigners over the government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy.

The decision will be made just as Andy Burnham prepares to travel to his first Cop summit as prime minister, where he and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will champion electrification on a global scale.

With some MPs already upset by the decisions to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and to cut funding for green schemes to pay for higher defence spending, many see the upcoming decisions on the Rosebank oilfield and the EV mandate as critically important.

Lizzi Collinge, the Labour MP for Morecambe and Lunesdale, said: “The upcoming decision on the ZEV [zero emission vehicle] mandate will have a huge climate impact, possibly the biggest one that’s on the PM’s desk.

“But it will also set the direction for tackling the cost of living and helping get our energy prices down over the coming decade.”

Catherine Fookes, the MP for Monmouthshire, said: “The government has some incredibly difficult decisions to make in the coming months and the prime minister will need to weigh up the consequences of each. We need the ZEV mandate to stay, and Rosebank to be rejected.”

A government spokesperson said: “The government is united in its commitment to the ZEV mandate and no decisions have been taken.

“We are committed to the phaseout of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets.

“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this, and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

Under rules brought in by the last Conservative government, carmakers have to make sure they only sell EVs by 2035, gradually increasing the proportion over time to 80% by 2030.

The policy is expected to create greater emissions savings than any other, leading to nearly 14% of all the reductions to which the UK has pledged between 2028 and 2032.

Carmakers have warned for years, however, that the interim targets in particular are unattainable, arguing that higher inflation and a squeeze on living standards have pushed them out of reach.

The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) says the industry will miss this year’s 33% target by a wide margin, with battery EVs accounting for 26.6% of new car sales in the first 10 months of the year.

Those targets, however, do not take into account exemptions that allow carmakers to avoid fines even if they undershoot their targets, such as by selling more hybrid cars, or making up for lower sales of electric cars now by selling more in the future.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The gap between demand and mandated targets continues to widen.

“Meaningful change to the trajectory, alongside expanded flexibilities throughout the regulation, is essential to bridge that gap, safeguard jobs and investment while keeping the UK’s zero emission transition on track.”

With ministers already having diluted the targets on multiple occasions since the policy was first proposed, the government launched another review into the policy in August, proposing five main options.

They were: to keep the mandate unchanged; keep it at 80% but extend the flexibilities by four years to 2034; reduce the interim target to 70%; reduce it to 60%; or reduce it to 50%.

That consultation kickstarted an internal battle in Whitehall. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has argued for the 2030 target to be reduced as far as possible, to 50%.

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, is believed to want it to be approximately 60%, while Miatta Fahnbulleh and her predecessor as energy secretary, Ed Miliband, are understood to want it to remain at 80%.

The prime minister would normally have sought to have resolved the dispute, but Burnham has recused himself from the decision because his wife, Marie-France van Heel, advises the board of the Manchester-based electric vehicle charging network Be.EV.

Government insiders say Haigh will probably sign off on a 2030 target of about 60%, while also extending the flexibilities in the targets until 2034. She is understood to have told colleagues, however, that she does not want them to come back in the future demanding another target reduction.

The decision will not only upset some Labour MPs, it will also dismay people in the wider environmental movement and in the EV charging industry, which is relying on high vehicle sales to recoup investment.

Shane Brennan, the chief executive of the trade association ChargeUK, said: “Weakening the mandate puts £1.7bn of charging infrastructure at risk and all the associated jobs and supply chain spending that goes with it.

“Charging investors’ confidence will be rocked by a third change in three years. Government should be in no way complacent about the long-term implications of being seen to cave to the short-term interest of global car importers.”

Paul McNamee, the director of the Labour Climate and Environment Forum, said: “Significant weakening of the ZEV mandate from the current 80% targets will be seen as a rowing back on climate leadership.

“If the government does this, it must provide assurance that the mandate will not be weakened again in the coming years, the 2035 target for EVs remains in place, and it delivers a robust industrial strategy to build a strong EV manufacturing base in the UK that will protect jobs in the long term.”

articles.summary: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said. articles.body:
Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. He said some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

More than 200,000 people have taken to the streets of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, demanding government action against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers.

Sunday’s ‘Red Line’ protesters, many wearing red items of clothing, called for tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.

“What is happening there is inhumane,” Mike van Dongen said as he walked in the huge throng of people.

“As far as I’m concerned, [the Dutch authorities] are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood at a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting, “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoed his cry as they passed.

At least 74,000 dead in Gaza

Israel’s genocidal war has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, since October 2023.

Sunday’s protest was similar to one in early October last year. That followed ‘Red Line’ demonstrations last June when protesters marched through the streets of The Hague.

A “ceasefire” took effect in Gaza on October 10 last year, but Israeli attacks and killings have continued on an almost-daily basis since.

The war in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel.

Since then, a new minority coalition government took power in February and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal – the ban provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly news conference on Friday.

“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said.

He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

articles.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
articles.summary: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.
articles.preview: South Africa's ANC hit by worst-ever performance in local elections November 8, 2026 The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages. South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a historically poor election performance, with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in Wednesday's municipal polls.
articles.body:
South Africa's ANC hit by worst-ever performance in local elections

November 8, 2026

The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a historically poor election performance, with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in Wednesday's municipal polls.

Their closes rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), won just under 25% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said on Saturday. With no outright winner declared in several major cities, politicians are expected enter tough coalition talks to form municipal governments.

ANC secretary general says outcome 'catastrophic'

While the ANC remains the most popular party in the country, they have been struggling with growing backlash from voters. In 2026, many South Africans are frustrated by water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities. High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are high on the public agenda.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has not yet addressed his party's poor performance. In his weekly presidential letter, however, he admitted that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

The ANC's steady decline with voters

The ANC had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela, the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

DA opposition holds large cities

The pro-business, center-right DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

articles.body:
El PSOE redirige la campaña hacia las cosas del comer. El ejemplo de las victorias progresistas en Estados Unidos y Brasil no ha acaparado el discurso de Pedro Sánchez en Bilbao en su tercer mitin consecutivo tras la suspensión de la precampaña por el accidente ferroviario de Urda. Por contra, el presidente del Gobierno se ha enfocado de nuevo en la gestión de los servicios públicos y la defensa del bienestar social.

Lo ha hecho asociando al PP y Vox a un retroceso en derechos y a futuros recortes, incidiendo en medidas ya anunciadas durante la semana, como la subida del salario mínimo (SMI) sin necesidad de una aprobación previa de la patronal —como dice el PP— y con compromisos muy concretos, como el blindaje de las pensiones en la Constitución y su revalorización conforme al IPC. Aunque todo ello dependerá de las mayorías en las Cortes Generales tras el 29-N, la promesa ha servido a Sánchez para arremeter contra el PP y Vox por las dudas que han planteado sobre el modelo vigente.

“Se lo vamos a exigir a todos los grupos parlamentarios, para que nadie vuelva a jugar con el futuro de las pensiones”, ha aseverado el candidato socialista ante 2.800 militantes y simpatizantes en el Palacio Euskalduna de Bilbao, este domingo. articles.title: ANC leads South Africa's local polls but records all-time election low: final results
articles.summary: The African National Congress came in first place in South Africa's local elections but suffered its worst-ever electoral setback, according to final results on Saturday.
articles.preview: South Africa The African National Congress came in first place in South Africa's local elections but suffered its worst-ever electoral setback, according to final results on Saturday. While still the largest party in the country, the once-dominant ANC has won just 32.5% of the vote. Frustrated voters have turned to the Democratic Alliance, the MK party and other smaller lists. The ANC's performance marks a drop of roughly 14 percentage points from its 2021 local election results.
articles.body:
South Africa

The African National Congress came in first place in South Africa's local elections but suffered its worst-ever electoral setback, according to final results on Saturday.

While still the largest party in the country, the once-dominant ANC has won just 32.5% of the vote.

Frustrated voters have turned to the Democratic Alliance, the MK party and other smaller lists.

The ANC's performance marks a drop of roughly 14 percentage points from its 2021 local election results.

The party has failed to win an outright majority in any of the eight metropolitan municipalities. But it finished ahead in four of them, including Johannesburg, Mangaung and Buffalo City.

The centre-right Democratic Alliance is the second-largest party, with about 22.9% of the vote. The party came first in Nelson Mandela Bay and Tshwane, and has secured a majority in Cape Town.

Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party is finishing in third place nationally with around 9.9% of the vote, and came first in the metro of eThekwini.

The results point to a fragmented political landscape. With the results now in, the parties will need to engage in coalition negotiations to form governing alliances.

With outright majorities elusive in several major cities, the results will usher in complex coalition negotiations as parties bargain to assemble the alliances needed to govern.

Such marriages of convenience have often proved unstable, leaving local administrations consumed by internal wrangling at the expense of basic service delivery.

The national government's existing coalition arrangements could further complicate negotiations, political analyst Daniel Silke told AFP.

Voters in Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and the capital Pretoria, would probably prefer to see the DA govern alongside centre-right ActionSA, he said.

"But the animosity between those two parties is extreme."

articles.body:
Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.

Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim, external reported.

The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.

The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.

The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.

However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.

Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".

The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.

Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.

Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.

Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.

The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker Türk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.

In August, Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.

Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.

The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

articles.title: Divided Israelis agree: Forming next government won't be easy
articles.summary: Across Israel people are divided over President Herzog’s decision to pick Gadi Eisenkot to lead country’s next government. But one thing everyone can agree on is that it forming a new government won't be easy.
articles.preview: Israel Across Israel people are divided over President Herzog’s decision to pick Gadi Eisenkot to lead country’s next government. The move was a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who lost his parliamentary majority in last month’s election. But one thing everyone can agree on is that it forming a new government won’t be easy. "I don't know what's going to be, but I want to give a blessing that there should be a new, a new understanding, a new mindset in Israel," says Jerusalem resident Nachman Horowitz.
articles.body:
Israel

Across Israel people are divided over President Herzog’s decision to pick Gadi Eisenkot to lead country’s next government.

The move was a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who lost his parliamentary majority in last month’s election.

But one thing everyone can agree on is that it forming a new government won’t be easy.

"I don't know what's going to be, but I want to give a blessing that there should be a new, a new understanding, a new mindset in Israel," says Jerusalem resident Nachman Horowitz.

"No matter what the government is, no matter what it is, that we should be able to look at one another, be able to respect one another, and that should be instead of focusing on a new government, it should be a new mentality, be able to look at every single person in Israel and be able to come to a new place of respect, of understanding. And that's the biggest thing that I hope will come with no matter what the political situation is.”

Eisenkot didn’t win a majority either. Arab-led parties meanwhile made historic gains leaving them as potential but politically complicated kingmakers.

"What are the challenges you need to overcome? Wow, there are many," says Anny Soronow, another Jerusalem resident.

"First of all, security. Second of all, to protect democracy. Third of all, to reverse the judicial revolution that (Benjamin Netanyahu) Bibi tried to do and then try to work with the with the one Arab party that will join the government hopefully. I have no problem with the Arabs being integrated into the government.”

Eisenkot has six weeks to form a new coalition. It’s a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the 2023 Hamas attacks and three years of war in Gaza and beyond.

The move comes despite a government report last week accusing the popular former mayor of financial improprieties.

articles.body:
Gambia

Supporters of Gambia’s UNITE-led coalition celebrated on Friday as their party leader Talib Ahmed Bensouda filed his candidacy papers for next month’s presidential election.

The move comes despite a government report last week accusing the popular former mayor of financial improprieties and abuse of office.

Bensouda's UNITE party has rejected the allegations as “a last-minute political manoeuvre intended to confuse the public…ahead of nominations.”

"The NPP government is desperate and afraid because they will lose this election", it said, referring to Barrow's National People's Party.

During his eight years as may of Kanifing Municipality, Bensouda gained a loyal following by implementing regular waste collection. His political star has continued to rise as the tiny west African nation faces prolonged blackouts.

The electricity cuts have led to numerous protests and calls for President Adama Barrow to step down.

The presidential election is scheduled for December 5, when Barrow will be running for a third term. While the list of election nominees has not yet been made official, leading opposition candidate Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, who ran against Barrow in 2021, has also said he will run.

If the allegations against Bensouda are proven, he would be disqualified from standing.

articles.title: Il mare che avanza
articles.summary: When the sea moves in è un progetto collettivo in cui fotografia e ricerca scientifica s’incontrano per raccontare i cambiamenti che stanno ridisegnando le coste italiane
articles.preview: Come si fotografa il mare? Come si può trasformare qualcosa in continuo movimento in un’immagine capace di raccontarlo e renderlo comprensibile? È quello che hanno provato a fare sei fotografi – Fabio Barile, Matteo de Mayda, Giorgio Di Noto, Amina Chouairi, Giulia Parlato e Massimo Sordi– con When the sea moves in, che indaga le trasformazioni delle coste italiane e i fenomeni che ne stanno modificando gli equilibri.
articles.body:
Come si fotografa il mare? Come si può trasformare qualcosa in continuo movimento in un’immagine capace di raccontarlo e renderlo comprensibile?

È quello che hanno provato a fare sei fotografi – Fabio Barile, Matteo de Mayda, Giorgio Di Noto, Amina Chouairi, Giulia Parlato e Massimo Sordi– con When the sea moves in, che indaga le trasformazioni delle coste italiane e i fenomeni che ne stanno modificando gli equilibri. Il lavoro fa dialogare fotografia e ricerca scientifica, ed è articolato in cinque progetti raccolti in altrettanti libri pubblicati da Witty Books.

Le coste del Mediterraneo sono ecosistemi fragili, minacciati dall’erosione, dai cambiamenti climatici e dalle attività umane. L’innalzamento del livello del mare, gli eventi meteorologici estremi, l’urbanizzazione e il turismo di massa stanno modificando il paesaggio costiero, mettendo a rischio non solo gli equilibri naturali, ma anche la biodiversità, le economie locali e il patrimonio culturale.

“Capire questi cambiamenti, ricostruirne le cause e seguirne l’evoluzione nel tempo è indispensabile per immaginare strategie di tutela e interventi di difesa sostenibili”, spiegano Stefania Rössl e Tommaso Parrillo, curatori del progetto. “Non si tratta solo di fotografare ciò che accade lungo le coste, ma di comprendere attraverso quali strumenti possiamo osservare e interpretare le trasformazioni in atto”.

A partire da questa riflessione ogni fotografo ha indagato un tratto del litorale italiano con il proprio linguaggio, concentrandosi su un aspetto preciso. In Atlas undarum Giulia Parlato osserva il mare attraverso esperimenti condotti in laboratorio, in cui il movimento delle onde è riprodotto in scala per studiare il modo in cui l’acqua interagisce con la costa e modifica la distribuzione dei sedimenti. Parlato fotografa questi ambienti trasformando vasche, materiali e movimenti dell’acqua in immagini che nella loro astrattezza a volte somigliano a dipinti. In altri casi realizza still life che rendono visibili processi che di norma lo sono solo per gli addetti ai lavori, mostrando gli strumenti attraverso cui la ricerca scientifica li studia.

Matteo de Mayda e Amina Chouairi in Lagoonal capriccio esplorano il paesaggio poco conosciuto della laguna di Venezia, in particolare le casse di colmata, isole artificiali nate per sostenere lo sviluppo industriale di Porto Marghera e successivamente abbandonate. Attraverso queste immagini, indagano il cambiamento di questi territori nel corso di più di sessant’anni, raccontando un ambiente fragile e in continua evoluzione, segnato dall’erosione provocata dal traffico navale e dalla progressiva trasformazione dell’ecosistema. Ne emerge una visione inedita della laguna, lontana dall’immaginario turistico di Venezia, che invita a riflettere sul rapporto tra esseri umani e natura.

In Layers di Giorgio Di Noto l’attenzione è di nuovo sui processi e sugli strumenti della ricerca scientifica. Il progetto si concentra sulle tecnologie e sui sistemi di osservazione usati per studiare l’erosione costiera, interpretarne i meccanismi e prevederne l’evoluzione.

Nel testo che apre il suo volume Among, Fabio Barile introduce il paesaggio del Lido di Ostia, al centro della sua ricerca, attraverso la descrizione di una scena apparentemente immobile: una superficie marina quasi piatta, lievemente increspata, una spiaggia sabbiosa e un uomo, il signor Array, seduto con le spalle rivolte al mare. Barile invita a osservare gli effetti del tempo sull’ambiente: le onde che consumano gli scogli, la pioggia che scava la pietra. Le sue immagini si concentrano sul progressivo deterioramento delle architetture balneari e sulla loro lenta trasformazione in sabbia, polvere e sedimento.

La serie Rivoluzione di Massimo Sordi prende invece in esame le falesie di Ortona, in Abruzzo, usandole come punto di osservazione del rapporto tra i fenomeni astronomici – come i movimenti dei corpi celesti e le loro interazioni gravitazionali – e i processi che trasformano la superficie terrestre – come l’erosione marina e il progressivo modellamento delle falesie.

Le immagini di questi lavori non formano una narrazione unica, ma costruiscono un insieme di osservazioni che mettono in relazione luoghi e modalità di conoscenza. Pur affrontando temi complessi e spesso molto tecnici, il progetto ha un intento divulgativo: attraverso la fotografia cerca di tradurre fenomeni scientifici in immagini e racconti accessibili a un pubblico più ampio, stimolando una maggiore consapevolezza delle trasformazioni delle coste del paesaggio mediterraneo.

articles.title: Come Cyndi Lauper e i Goonies inventarono gli anni ottanta
articles.summary: Una canzone dimenticata e un film che è diventato un oggetto di culto per generazioni diverse
articles.preview: Rimettendo in ordine i dischi ho ripescato un vecchio 45 giri, uno dei primi che avevo comprato con i miei soldi quando ero ragazzino. Su una facciata c’è una canzone pop confezionata per un film di Hollywood; sull’altra un rockabilly un po’ sgangherato intitolato What a thrill, “che sballo”. Le canta entrambe Cyndi Lauper, una delle popstar più famose della metà degli anni ottanta. Il pezzo sul lato A, The Goonies ’r’ good enough, accompagnava I Goonies, un film d’avventura del 1985 diretto da Richard Donner e prodotto da Steven Spielberg.
articles.body:
Rimettendo in ordine i dischi ho ripescato un vecchio 45 giri, uno dei primi che avevo comprato con i miei soldi quando ero ragazzino. Su una facciata c’è una canzone pop confezionata per un film di Hollywood; sull’altra un rockabilly un po’ sgangherato intitolato What a thrill, “che sballo”. Le canta entrambe Cyndi Lauper, una delle popstar più famose della metà degli anni ottanta. Il pezzo sul lato A, The Goonies ’r’ good enough, accompagnava I Goonies, un film d’avventura del 1985 diretto da Richard Donner e prodotto da Steven Spielberg. Quella canzone arrivò a lambire la Top 10 statunitense: un risultato discreto per un’artista ormai abituata da almeno due anni ai piani più alti delle classifiche pop. Poi, mentre il film cominciava una sua strana vita carsica da oggetto di culto, la canzone scivolava ai margini del repertorio della sua interprete. Fino a finire quasi dimenticata.

Quelle due canzoni (Goonies e What a thrill) sono rimaste incastrate tra She’s so unusual, l’album d’esordio che aveva trasformato Lauper in una star, e True colors, l’album che nel 1986 avrebbe consolidato il suo successo. Nessuna delle due trovò posto in quei dischi. The Goonies ’r’ good enough rimase fuori anche da Twelve deadly Cyns, la sua prima raccolta di successi del 1994. Sarebbe riapparsa in The essential Cyndi Lauper nel 2003, ma ormai era diventata una curiosità laterale: il tema di un film per ragazzi nella carriera di una cantante e autrice di cui perfino un genio indiscusso del novecento come Miles Davis aveva riconosciuto il talento autoriale, incidendo Time after time nel 1985.

Eppure quel piccolo disco dimenticato, con le sue due facciate così diverse, racconta parecchio di Cyndi Lauper. E forse ancora di più degli anni ottanta: anni che le generazioni millennial e post-millennial hanno ricostruito e reinventato riscoprendo e amando anche un film minore come I Goonies.

A metà degli anni ottanta Lauper sembrava fatta apposta per accompagnare una banda di ragazzini un po’ strani, goffi e fuori posto come i Goonies. Anche lei aveva costruito il proprio personaggio di oddball, di eccentrica, mettendo insieme apparentemente a casaccio vestiti da mercatino dell’usato, capelli di tutti i colori, una voce capace di passare dal singhiozzo alla risata, dal cinguettio di un canarino a un registro più alto e pieno, quasi da cantante soul. Perché Cyndi Lauper è sempre stata, a differenza di altre star della sua epoca, anzitutto una cantante. La sua personalità in bilico tra comico e malinconico conservava qualcosa di popolare e sfrontato. E il suo look rattoppato, che univa certe ingenuità hippy a qualche spigolo punk, era pensato per l’estetica frenetica e fluorescente della prima era di Mtv. Nel mondo dei Goonies, dove dei piccoli esclusi diventano eroi di cappa e spada, Cyndi poteva entrare senza neanche cambiarsi. Le bastava essere lei.

La sua canzone, però, che originariamente s’intitolava solo Good enough, non raccontava l’avventura dei Goonies. Era una canzone che parlava di rapporti complicati, aspettative difficili da conciliare con la vita reale. Il ritornello cercava un accordo possibile: quello che va abbastanza bene per te va abbastanza bene anche per me. Insomma: accontentiamoci di quello che abbiamo anche se a volte può sembrare un po’ un casino.

È buffo come certe espressioni tornino a galla nei decenni, ma con significati diversi. Un po’ come i Goonies sono riemersi nell’immaginario collettivo grazie a un bizzarro fenomeno di passaparola intergenerazionale, così l’espressione good enough sarebbe diventata anche una formula tecnologica. Nel 2009 la rivista Wired descriveva la rivoluzione dell’“abbastanza buono”: mp3, chiamate Skype, video compressi e sgranati spesso interrotti dal buffering. Una qualità imperfetta, compensata dalla comodità, dal basso costo e dalla portabilità: “What is good enough for you is good enough for me”, proprio come cantava Cyndi Lauper.

Il suono dell’avventura

L’arrangiamento, con quelle percussioni riverberate e quei tastieroni così anni ottanta, faceva sembrare tutto più semplice. Quel riff di tastiera iniziale che imita il suono della marimba era un facile escamotage sonoro per farci entrare subito nel contesto esotico di un’avventura un po’ da isola del tesoro. Negli anni ottanta il suono del synth che imitava marimba, vibrafoni o gamelan era un suono “finto” che suggeriva un’idea astratta di oriente misterioso: i Japan e David Sylvian lo usavano con classe e poesia in pezzi come Canton del 1981, gli Alphaville in Big in Japan o Murray Head in One night in Bangkok, entrambi del 1984, lo usavano in modo più furbetto ed esotizzante, proprio come lo usava Cyndi in The Goonies ’r’ good enough.

Il titolo della canzone da Good enough e basta fu allungato in The Goonies ’r’ good enough per legarla indissolubilmente al film, con grande irritazione dell’autrice. È per questo che un brano arrivato al numero dieci negli Stati Uniti sarebbe rimasto a lungo ai margini del suo repertorio: era la stessa Cyndi a detestare la canzone e il costosissimo video promozionale che l’accompagnava.

Il video di The Goonies ’r’ good enough era una piccola follia diretta da Donner e divisa in due puntate. Cyndi Lauper, più clownesca e svitata che mai, deve salvare la stazione di servizio della sua famiglia dalle mire di alcuni creditori. Per riuscirci si infila in un’avventura sotterranea, tra pirati e trappole, incontrando i ragazzi dei Goonies e le Bangles, all’epoca pronte a fare il loro grande salto nel mainstream del pop con pezzi come Manic monday e Walk like an egyptian.

I cattivi hanno le facce e i muscoli dei wrestler: tra le varie attività imprenditoriali di Cyndi Lauper in quel periodo c’era anche quella di manager di alcuni lottatori professionisti. Nel video compare perfino il vero Steven Spielberg: Cyndi gli chiede aiuto gridando mentre si trova su un ponte di corda circondata da pirati ed energumeni, ma neanche lui sa come tirarla fuori dai guai. Cinema, Mtv, musica pop e wrestling convergono in uno stesso spettacolo, con l’esuberanza di un’industria che sta scoprendo quanto pubblico si possa raggiungere mettendo tutto insieme nello stesso frullatore.

Sotto tutto quel chiasso c’è una paura concreta. La famiglia di Cyndi nel video è sgangherata, chiassosa, poco presentabile; sembrano tutti usciti da un film di John Waters se mai John Waters avesse fatto film per famiglie. Cyndi sa bene che chi ha i soldi può portarle via il posto in cui vive e lavora. La paura di restare senza nulla è anche il motore del film dei Goonies, i cui protagonisti cercano un tesoro per impedire che le loro case siano demolite per fare spazio a un campo da golf.

In entrambe le storie l’avventura nasce da una minaccia immobiliare. E in entrambe, per difendere la propria vita bisogna diventare ricchi. L’amicizia dà il coraggio di scendere nelle caverne; per fermare i creditori servono i gioielli del tesoro sepolto. Il denaro compra la possibilità di restare dove si è. Insomma, gli anni ottanta concentrati in poche righe di sinossi.

Cyndi Lauper canta dal vivo What a thrill, il pezzo che sarebbe finito sulla facciata B del 45 giri dei Goonies

Alla fine, quegli anni erano proprio questo: la fantasia che un colpo di fortuna possa sottrarti al potere dei soldi degli altri. Riguardando i Goonies e il video di Cyndi Lauper attraverso il filtro della nostalgia, è facile ricordare le biciclette, gli amici e un’infanzia apparentemente libera, lasciando sullo sfondo l’angoscia economica.

I Goonies hanno raggiunto molti millennial attraverso fratelli maggiori, cugini, genitori e videocassette viste fino a consumarle. Il passaggio generazionale era cominciato molto prima di Stranger things, che nel 2016 avrebbe ripreso quella formula di amicizia, pericolo e avventura trasformandola in un nuovo racconto degli anni ottanta. Un nuovo racconto in cui la questione dei soldi rimaneva sullo sfondo ma rimaneva.

“Ma da quando i Goonies è diventato un bel film?”

In Giovani si diventa, un film del 2014 diretto da Noah Baumbach, parlando di un ragazzo che accosta I Goonies a Quarto potere, un personaggio chiede: “Ma da quando I Goonies è diventato un bel film?”. La battuta coglie lo scarto tra un giudizio sul cinema e l’affetto per un oggetto culturale cresciuto insieme a chi lo guarda e custodito come un prezioso ricordo d’infanzia. Per Brian Eggert, che firma un lungo pezzo sui Goonies su Deep Focus Review, rivederlo è “un esercizio di nostalgia avvolto in altra nostalgia”.

Quando Steven Spielberg, nel 1981, girava I predatori dell’arca perduta faceva già un esercizio di nostalgia: si ricollegava a certi fumetti d’avventura della sua infanzia, così come Umberto Eco in quegli stessi anni rivalutava i fumetti degli anni trenta con cui lui era cresciuto e che, come tutti i bambini della sua generazione, era costretto a leggere di nascosto. Gli anni ottanta sono stati anni di cannibalesco consumo d’infanzie perdute: dal grottesco e opulento Flash Gordon del 1980 diretto da Mike Hodges con la colonna sonora dei Queen, al meraviglioso, terribile mondo parallelo di Watchmen creato nel 1986 dal fumettista Alan Moore, in cui i supereroi degli anni quaranta e cinquanta ormai invecchiati non erano riusciti a cambiare né il mondo né se stessi.

The Goonies ’r’ good enough, quel polveroso 45 giri di Cyndi Lauper recuperato facendo le pulizie, è un frammento di questa storia: un decennio che rimasticava le infanzie dei padri per fabbricare quelle dei figli. Questi ultimi avrebbero poi fatto lo stesso, passando ad altri bambini le proprie avventure e trasformando un film di pirati e una canzone pop in ricordi di famiglia. A ogni passaggio qualcosa si conserva e qualcosa si perde. Restano le biciclette, il tesoro, l’amicizia; ma restano anche i debiti, la paura di perdere la casa e quell’idea deleteria della ricchezza vista come premio e come talismano che è forse l’eredità più autentica e problematica degli anni ottanta.

Cyndi Lauper

The Goonies ’r’ good enough/ What a thrill

articles.title: Iran threatens to ‘rain down hell’ if US escalates war
articles.summary: President Trump warns that US forces are 'locked and loaded' and ready to strike, if necessary.
articles.preview: US President Donald Trump warns that United States forces are ‘locked and loaded’ and ready to strike if necessary. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the United States resumes attacks, serving Washington with an ultimatum in an attempt to end the two countries’ eight-month war. “Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Araghchi wrote in a post on X on Sunday.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump warns that United States forces are ‘locked and loaded’ and ready to strike if necessary.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the United States resumes attacks, serving Washington with an ultimatum in an attempt to end the two countries’ eight-month war.

“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Araghchi wrote in a post on X on Sunday.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened warriors rain down hell,” he said.

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that renewed strikes on Iran are “highly unlikely” if negotiations progress over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

‘Locked and loaded’

“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said when asked about continued US strikes on Iran during a phone interview reported by CNN. “I would [continue], if necessary, but we hit them really hard,” he added.

Trump warned that US forces have three aircraft carriers stationed in the region “fully locked and loaded”, ready to continue strikes if need be. He also said that the US has 38 bridges in Iran’s crosshairs that US forces “can knock down in literally one hour”.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry also quoted Araghchi in an earlier statement on Sunday that said Iran would “not go easy on American targets” in the region.

Araghchi’s statements came after reports by state media that an oil tanker caught fire earlier that morning after hitting a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz, citing Iran’s navy.

The navy claimed the ship’s identification systems were turned off and it was travelling in the no-go zone of the strait.

‘Devastating and severe’ response

An adviser to Iran’s commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Aerospace Force made threats that echoed those of the Iranian foreign minister and said that weapons have been “secured for years to come”.

“The armed forces are at the ready, and if the enemy makes a mistake, Iran’s response will be devastating and severe,” warned IRGC Brigadier-General Ali Belali in a statement on Telegram.

“As senior commanders of the armed forces have pointed out, we have upgraded our capabilities in the post-Ramadan War period,” Belali said.

The back-and-fourth between Iranian and US leaders comes following US midterm elections in which the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress, soundly defeating Trump’s Republican Party.

Araghchi alleged that negotiations have been delayed as a result of the elections, but he awaits the path forward, Iranian state media reported.

“It will take some time for things to settle down and for the atmosphere to become conducive to the mediators resuming their visits,” the foreign minister said. “We have to wait.”

articles.title: Ucraina: Europei e Francia al trilaterale di Abu Dhabi, ma i Volenterosi si esercitano
articles.summary: Da lunedì in Polonia manovre militari per il dopo guerra in Ucraina. 'Raid su soccorsi'
articles.preview: Alla vigilia dell'incontro tecnico ad Abu Dhabi, il trilaterale tra Russia, Ucraina e Usa si trasforma in un multilaterale allargandosi al vecchio continente, che tuttavia non rinuncia a lanciare quasi contemporaneamente le prime esercitazioni dei Volenterosi pro Kiev, in Polonia. È stato il ministro degli Esteri francese Jean-Noël Barrot a rompere il velo di riservatezza sul cambio di format: "Gli europei saranno adeguatamente rappresentati e la Francia sarà ad Abu Dhabi per partecipare a queste discussioni", ha dichiarato.
articles.body:
Alla vigilia dell'incontro tecnico ad Abu Dhabi, il trilaterale tra Russia, Ucraina e Usa si trasforma in un multilaterale allargandosi al vecchio continente, che tuttavia non rinuncia a lanciare quasi contemporaneamente le prime esercitazioni dei Volenterosi pro Kiev, in Polonia.

È stato il ministro degli Esteri francese Jean-Noël Barrot a rompere il velo di riservatezza sul cambio di format: "Gli europei saranno adeguatamente rappresentati e la Francia sarà ad Abu Dhabi per partecipare a queste discussioni", ha dichiarato. "Non posso ancora dirvi chi rappresenterà la Francia in quell' occasione, ma la Francia ci sarà", ha proseguito.

"Ci sono state discussioni, a volte senza gli europei, a volte con loro. Questa volta vi parteciperanno. La Francia sarà presente e farà sentire la voce dell'Europa", ha assicurato il titolare del Quai d' Orsay, che nelle grandi crisi internazionali tende a promuovere il formato E3 (Francia, Germania, Gb) in coordinamento con la responsabile della diplomazia europea Kaja Kallas.

L'annuncio arriva pochi giorni dopo che la premier Giorgia Meloni ha denunciato in una lettera al presidente del Consiglio Ue Antonio Costa l'approccio "in ordine sparso" dei Paesi europei nei negoziati sull'Ucraina, rilanciando la "necessità ormai improcrastinabile" per la Ue "di parlare con una sola voce" su questo conflitto. Nella lettera Meloni aveva elencato i troppi formati degli ultimi tempi e aveva detto di aver saputo di "una non meglio precisata presenza europea ai colloqui previsti ad Abu Dhabi tra ucraini e russi con la mediazione americana".

Presenza che rimane imprecisata anche dopo l'uscita di Barrot. Pure Jared Kushner, inviato di Trump nonché suo genero, aveva ventilato giovedì scorso un allargamento del formato agli europei, ma subordinato ad eventuali passi avanti nei negoziati: gli Stati Uniti, aveva detto, "si consulteranno strettamente con i loro partner europei" a margine dei colloqui di Abu Dhabi e "qualora si registrassero dei progressi, l'obiettivo sarà quello di evolvere verso un formato multilaterale più ampio, con la loro partecipazione diretta".

I colloqui negli Emirati Arabi dovrebbero consentire di delineare una possibile via d'uscita dal conflitto, con un accordo che, secondo Donald Trump, "potrebbe coinvolgere l'intera Europa". Gli europei e Kiev hanno però messo in guardia contro qualsiasi ipotesi di un'"architettura di sicurezza" che venisse delineata alle loro spalle. Kushner, secondo il Washington Post, punterebbe a un modello tipo il Consiglio Nato-Russia, istituito dopo la Guerra Fredda ma sospeso nel 2014, in seguito all'annessione della Crimea.

Nel frattempo, lunedì partono le prime esercitazioni militari della Forza multinazionale per l'Ucraina (Mnf-u), il "braccio militare" dei Volenterosi in vista del dopoguerra: principalmente in Polonia, ma, come spiegato dal generale di Corpo d'Armata britannico Bateman, responsabile dell' addestramento 'Koalicja', anche in Turchia e Francia. In campo, sino al 22 novembre, 2.800 soldati, di cui circa 1.100 francesi, 300 britannici e gli altri appartenenti agli eserciti di Belgio, Estonia, Germania, Lituania, Paesi Bassi, Polonia, Spagna, Svezia e Turchia.

E mentre i dem vittoriosi a Midterm stanno cercando di mettere insieme un nuovo pacchetto di aiuti da 15 miliardi per Kiev, Mosca continua ad attaccare l'Ucraina: anche a Komyshuvakha, "dove da sette giorni sono in corso operazioni di soccorso dopo un bombardamento che ha ucciso 55 persone", ha denunciato Zelensky parlando di "un cinismo e una crudeltà assoluti". L'offensiva russa però paga un prezzo umano altissimo sul fronte terrestre: secondo i dati rubati all'agenzia di statistica russa Rosstat dal gruppo bielorusso filo-opposizione Cyber Partisans e dagli hacker ucraini Silent Crow, fra il febbraio 2022 e la fine di agosto 2026 sono stati registrati 392.700 certificati di morte legati esplicitamente alla guerra in Ucraina.

articles.preview: Former military chief says prime minister brought Israel to historic crisis and it is approaching ‘point of no return’ Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis.
articles.body:
Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis.

Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority.

“We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the state of Israel,” said Eisenkot, who had traded his usual all black for a suit and tie at a ceremony at the presidential office. “We must form a national emergency government. This will require creative and unconventional political steps.”

Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.

Eisenkot and Herzog acknowledged Israel’s growing isolation under Netanyahu, who is wanted by the international criminal court.

In the US, Israel’s closest ally, Democrats on Tuesday swept the midterm elections, with calls to rein in Israel after the devastation in Gaza and the unpopular Iran war, which Netanyahu launched with Donald Trump.

Eisenkot said: “We are in the midst of a devastating diplomatic crisis. Even our closest friends and strategic allies are saying their relationship with Israel must be reassessed.”

He appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud party as well as the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, to join him – but only with himself as prime minister.

“My door is open and my hand is extended, wholeheartedly and willingly, to anyone who understands the gravity of this moment,” he said.

Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.

Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in the October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.

During party consultations with Herzog, Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.

Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of his partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, has already said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.

Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims.

Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Committee – and Herzog – say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing was found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.

Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night but it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement. These types of coalition governments are notoriously fragile and often collapse.

Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.

He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.

He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and has vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.

Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.

After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.

If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.

articles.title: US task force to cut off Iran’s transport of advanced weapons: What we know
articles.summary: As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces 'Task Force Iron Gate'.
articles.preview: As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces ‘Task Force Iron Gate’. As the threat of renewed war grows, Washington is expanding efforts to choke Tehran’s military supply networks, including through Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea. With it, the US military is trying to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday.
articles.body:
As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces ‘Task Force Iron Gate’.

As the threat of renewed war grows, Washington is expanding efforts to choke Tehran’s military supply networks, including through Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea.

With it, the US military is trying to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday.

The same day, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced ambitious plans for underground complexes capable of sustaining missile and drone production under bombardment. That announcement came amid reports of ongoing construction near Iranian missile bases, based on satellite imagery and previous claims by Tehran that US strikes failed to destroy its underground facilities.

Here’s what we know about the US task force:

What is the purpose of the task force?

Task Force Iron Gate will aim to find out where “weapons systems are coming in, how they could potentially be cut off” and how “Iran is transporting its energy”, Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

It expands on the US blockade of Iranian ports to cover Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea and will reportedly be run by 20 civilian and military personnel.

Iran shares borders with seven countries – Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan Turkiye and Turkmenistan.

Based in Tampa, Florida, the unit will coordinate with other US government agencies “on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea”, CENTCOM said. Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea”, CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

If US President Donald Trump ramps up the war, there will likely be attacks on this “series of targets”, said Mulroy.

“Unlike Operation Epic Fury, which primarily (focused) on military targets, I think these targets will be focused on economic and infrastructure targets, as part of this comprehensive plan to cut the regime off from its ability to fight and ability to fund itself,” Mulroy said. “It’s primarily a coordination body that’s looking for how the US can increase its economic strangulation strategy by going after the ground routes as they’ve already covered a majority of the maritime routes.”

How has Iran responded to CENTCOM’s announcement?

The IRGC dismissed the US military plan as “just a play on words”.

“The Americans cannot achieve their goal through this, which is to apply severe economic pressure to collapse and disintegrate the Iranian economy,” said IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi, as reported by the Fars news agency.

Washington previously “claimed that Iran will suffer an economic collapse within two weeks, but we witnessed that this did not happen”, he added.

Is the task force a response to reports of Russia-Iran weapons ties?

While CENTCOM’s announcement did not explicitly identify Iran’s weapons trade with Russia, analysts say the unit could be seen as an attempt to disrupt supply networks that include Russian connections.

US media have reported that Russia has sent drone components and explosives to Iran via the Caspian Sea. There are also claims that Russian technology could be helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles.

Mahjoob Zweiri, a professor of contemporary history and politics at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that reports of military equipment imported via Russia are a “real concern” for the United States.

The task force therefore could “cause a confrontation with Russia”, he said.

Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut and a non-resident senior fellow at the Arab Center in Washington, said of the new unit: “The US really doesn’t quite know what to do about Iran as we’ve seen, and it’s doing things off the cuff” – a strategy that has led to little success.

Can the US really choke off Iran’s supply lines?

Khouri pointed to Iran’s history as a trading nation for thousands of years as evidence that the US mission is near impossible.

“There’s an enormous web of contacts that Iran has had for thousands of years with traders and partners and allies all over the region, especially in Asia – it’s virtually impossible for the US to seal off every one,” he said.

While the US can impose a blockade or sanctions on Iran, it cannot control the behaviour of everyone from the Russians, to the Chinese, to the Emiratis and beyond, said the analyst.

“There are people all over the region who have links with Iran, some very close, some just commercial,” he said.

A lot of the materials that go into Iran’s weapons systems are bought from some other countries, – some even from the US or Europeans – and then they are channelled through companies in Asia, Khouri added.

Could this change the course of the war?

Former Trump aide and top counterterrorism official Joe Kent, who resigned in March due to the US’s war on Iran, said the new task force is an attempt by CENTCOM to subvert ongoing diplomatic efforts.

“This is CENTCOM inviting Iran to escalate while the vice president is attempting to negotiate with the Iranians,” Kent posted on X. “This is, as CENTCOM calls it, ‘policy by CONOP’, when the military finds a way to subvert the White House without blatantly disobeying the President, by taking actions that will ensure a war escalates or perpetuates.”

According to The Wall Street Journal, CENTCOM chief Cooper is among the many officials, alongside Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing Trump to renew attacks on Iran.

The task force may also just be symbolic because the US has no military presence on the Caspian Sea, said Zweiri.

“America has no access to the sea, unless some of the neighbouring countries like Azerbaijan or Armenia or others collaborate [with them] … And they’re not collaborating on this because they don’t want to upset Russia,” he said. “It will require … troops on the ground, and this is unlikely to happen.”

Zweiri also said that the Caspian Sea’s contribution to Iran’s economy is just 11 percent, so the task force’s actions won’t have much negative impact on Tehran.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify this figure but the Caspian Sea accounts for only a fraction of Iran’s overall maritime trade, according to the Soufan Center based in New York City.

articles.summary: Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water.
articles.preview: Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water. JAKARTA: A crew member of a helicopter battling Indonesian wildfires was killed on Sunday (Nov 8) when the aircraft crashed into a river as it scooped up water for an airborne drop, a local disaster agency said.
articles.body:
Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water.

JAKARTA: A crew member of a helicopter battling Indonesian wildfires was killed on Sunday (Nov 8) when the aircraft crashed into a river as it scooped up water for an airborne drop, a local disaster agency said.

The crash in Borneo Island's South Kalimantan province was the second in days involving a firefighting aircraft, after a military helicopter plunged into the waters off Borneo on Wednesday, killing three people.

Two Australian pilots survived Sunday's crash and were "safe", Berton Panjaitan, a spokesman for the national disaster mitigation agency, told AFP earlier on Sunday. Further details of their condition were not immediately available.

Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downward after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water.

"A joint search and rescue team recovered the final victim at 6:08 pm local time during a diving operation involving four divers," a statement released by the search and rescue office in provincial capital Banjarmasin on Sunday evening said.

The Southeast Asian archipelago has been struggling for months to control blazes that have burned through large swaths of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua islands, causing choking haze that drifted to neighbouring Malaysia, East Timor and Singapore.

"This incident occurred while the air fleet was conducting a water-bombing operation," spokesman Berton told AFP.

The Eurocopter EC225LP Super Puma belonged to a company the disaster mitigation agency had contracted for water-bombing operations, he said.

On Wednesday, a helicopter carrying eight people crashed during a mission to fight fires in Tanjung Puting National Park, home to animals including critically endangered Bornean orangutans.

That crash also occurred while the aircraft was scooping seawater for water bombing, according to an army statement that said the cause was under investigation.

Aside from ground-based firefighters, Indonesia has relied heavily on air operations to fight the fires that have destroyed more than 1.9 million hectares, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas.

The fires are driven in part by a strong El Nino weather phenomenon, which in Indonesia typically causes drought.

articles.title: Russian strikes wound nine and damage Ukraine's power network ahead of talks
articles.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

articles.body:
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.

Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.

Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.

The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".

Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.

"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.

The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.

Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.

The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.

She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.

Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.

He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.

"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."

Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
