articles.body:
Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.

The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.

Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms.

Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.

Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.

In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.

Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.

Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.

In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.

Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.

Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.

The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.

It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.

The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.

The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

articles.body:
Il 18 ottobre 2026 su X è stato condiviso un post contenente un collage di otto foto, scattate in diversi momenti, di funerali di otto soldati ucraini. In ognuna di queste immagini compare lo stesso bambino, con un’espressione triste, che tiene in mano di volta in volta la foto del soldato ucciso in guerra.

Secondo chi l’ha condivisa, il bambino sarebbe stato presentato come lo stesso figlio di otto soldati differenti. Quindi si sarebbe di una messinscena ucraina per ingannare i media internazionali.

È un contenuto presentato in maniera fuorviante, che diffonde una notizia falsa.

Come hanno verificato diversi siti di fact-checking internazionali in precedenza, tutte le foto mostrate nel collage sono state pubblicate tra ottobre 2025 e gennaio 2026 dalla pagina Facebook ufficiale del villaggio ucraino di Otynia, situato nell’Ucraina occidentale. Sono scatti che immortalano funerali di soldati ucraini uccisi nella guerra d’invasione russa. Nelle condivisioni originarie delle foto, il bambino con in mano la foto del defunto non viene mai presentato come il figlio dei vari soldati uccisi.

Contattato dai fact-checker di AFP, un funzionario locale di Otynia aveva spiegato a febbraio 2026 che il bambino ritratto aveva scelto di partecipare ai funerali volontariamente. All’epoca la stessa pagina Facebook di Otynia aveva confermato che il bambino in questione «è un residente del luogo che partecipa ai funerali degli Eroi caduti per propria iniziativa, portandone i ritratti come gesto di rispetto e gratitudine».

articles.title: Nvidia says it’s investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
articles.summary: In a memo to the company, Huang admitted that he had an affair.
articles.preview: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a Chinese spy operation. Bloomberg and other outlets reported that Huang sent a message to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. A memo circulated among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a Chinese spy operation.

Bloomberg and other outlets reported that Huang sent a message to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. A memo circulated among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang added that he’d “fallen short’ of his responsibility to the company.

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.

AI chips, including those created by Nvidia, have been a focus in the trade war between the United States and China. Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI industry (though he doesn’t want us to call it AI).

In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security nor company secrets were compromised, and that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” The board also said it has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel.

In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.

Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies, including those offering sex or romance.

Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. A statement posted by the board of directors reads:

Following reports that Nvidia’s CEO had a ‘close relationship’ with an AI exec the company is opening an investigation.

The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.

The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.

The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.

The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing.

Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. Both the Biden and Trump administrations have restricted their sale to China. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips.

Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

articles.body:
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals.

Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks.

Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months. One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs. Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3. The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman. That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.

But that’s just the start. Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs. Gurman says:

Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

articles.title: He arrested a hacker, then spent 18 months clearing his own name. Now he’s a cybersecurity VC.
articles.summary: Stephen Ward, a former Secret Service agent and Home Depot CISO, is preparing a second fund of roughly $250 million for Brightmind Partners.
articles.preview: Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO. Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says. Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out.
articles.body:
Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO.

Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says.

Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his résumé, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing.

One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A.

Now Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade.

His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue.

Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.”

After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 résumés but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first.

The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.)

What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it.

By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “Operation Firewall.”

Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.”

Six years as CISO at the financial services company TIAA followed, and then two years at Home Depot starting in 2019. But in 2021, feeling burned out, he quit without anything lined up for the first time since age 16.

That chapter didn’t last long. The founders of Wiz, whose security software Ward had used at Home Depot, put him on a short list for a job at their company. Jeff Horing, a venture capitalist at Insight Partners, which had co-led Wiz’s $100 million Series A round in late 2020, interviewed Ward for the role, then offered him one at Insight instead.

It’s a good-news, bad-news story, given that Wiz was acquired last year by Google for $32 billion. When I asked him about it last week, Ward observed that the friend who took the Wiz job “made life-changing money,” but said it doesn’t bother him.

Regardless, he spent just three years at Insight, where he says he worked on Wiz, Abnormal Security, and Elisity, which IonQ agreed in October to buy for up to $1.3 billion. Then, at age 49, he thought about striking out on his own for the first time.

He says people told him it was a young man’s game. He left anyway and began cold-emailing limited partners. Ultimately, fewer than 20 LPs filled the fund, including Horing.

Ward started Brightmind in 2024 with Talpaz, a CrowdStrike corporate development executive whose deals overlapped with Ward’s during his time at Insight. Tayler Sipperly, another CrowdStrike corporate development alum, was the firm’s third employee.

The partnership ended this past spring. Asked what happened, Ward, using carefully worded legalese, cited “differences in opinions regarding operations and the future of Brightmind.” In August, Talpaz and Sipperly co-founded a new venture firm with Elia Zaitsev, CrowdStrike’s global CTO for the past three years. Called Cognition, it’s now reportedly targeting a $170 million first fund to back cybersecurity startups.

Sipperly says that he and Talpaz “continue to support the existing Brightmind portfolio companies as well as its limited partners” and that they “remain on the board of a number of the Brightmind portfolio companies.”

Brightmind’s first fund has made 14 investments to date, with one exit: that SNGL sale.

Some investors asked why Brightmind didn’t ride out that bet even longer. But Ward says he’s seen enough across his career that he feels confident in warning founders when they’re “going to race past the turn.”

In cybersecurity, he says, the best sales come between a startup’s third and seventh years. Indeed, he says his team tracks every security acquisition and what buyers are building versus buying. If Palo Alto Networks is likely to buy something, he says, CrowdStrike will experience “FOMO, then Zscaler is going to look over and go, ‘What did they just do? I should probably do the same thing.’”

Understanding how the pieces fit together is the trick, Ward explained, offering some hypotheticals. If CrowdStrike is building a product, he said, it’s unlikely to buy a portfolio company that makes something similar. Palo Alto Networks might love a company, but not if buying it would force its customers to switch away from something it bought five years ago.

“It’s very easy to go, ‘Good match,’ ‘terrible match,’” he said. “And that’s really what we spend a ton of time figuring out.”

He has timing on his side, at least. Early-stage cybersecurity startups are outraising their later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade, according to PitchBook, which counts $4.7 billion worth of seed-through-Series B deals through September.

That total is already ahead of the entirety of 2025, even though the number of deals fell to 248 from 358 last year. Seed rounds in particular are ballooning, per PitchBook. The average cybersecurity seed round jumped to $8.4 million in the first nine months of this year, from $5.54 million a year earlier.

Ward questions how much of that money is really going to AI security. By PitchBook’s count, 278 deals in the first half of 2026 were bucketed as such, but his team’s manual review found only 30 true ones. He doesn’t think Anthropic or OpenAI will “take over the security world,” but instead will do “just enough.”

For real-time protection, which he terms “zero second,” he favors cyber-specific models that run locally on a customer’s own systems, like that of Empirical Security. He also looks for startups that could trounce established companies that he considers vulnerable, name-checking 27-year-old Qualys and 24-year-old Tenable.

Ward says Brightmind’s second fund won’t be entirely cybersecurity, focusing about 20% on AI infrastructure deals. He expects a meaningful number of teams to come from Israel, too. (Roughly 40% of the debut fund’s startups are based in Tel Aviv.)

Asked about the founders he’s most comfortable backing, the response is immediate: second-time founders who stick together.

Brightmind is comprised of five people right now: COO Iva Messy, also a Seton Hall graduate, came from venture firms Felicis and Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) on the recommendation of Ward’s cousin, Carl Eschenbach, a former Workday CEO who is now back at Sequoia. Sven Wollschlaeger, a Midwesterner whom Ward calls one of the hardest-working people he’s known, spent three years alongside Ward at Insight and is a principal at Brightmind.

CTO Jamie Mneimneh, whom Ward first hired at Home Depot as a distinguished engineer, is the most technical person of the team. He built the cloud computing environment on AWS where the firm tests startups’ products. Mneimneh also built the AI agents that now source most of Brightmind’s deal flow, which is how the firm avoids hiring a bench of analysts and keeps management fees down, says Ward.

Taylor Cleveland, Ward’s chief of staff at Home Depot, joined the firm a few months ago.

For all the career changes, Ward says the real force driving him hasn’t changed. He grew up without money and still worries it could happen again, saying he’s being paid to produce a “3x net fund,” and he’s “not going to celebrate until we get that.”

Said Ward: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have a level of being very naive to like, not being qualified to do something. I’ve just always looked at people and been like, ‘Okay, you know more than me today, but tomorrow, it’s going to be a little less, and the day after that, it’s going to be less, and eventually, I’m going to catch you and surpass you, and I’m going to know more than you.’ That’s how competitive I am.”

Update: Comments from Sipperly were added after publication.

Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub. There’s a flag listed for a “Conversational Apps” category. While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView. Code in iOS 27.3 has a flag for ‘Conversational Apps.’

Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts. It will also have a lockout system with increasingly longer wait times, starting at one hour for the second lockout, and climbing to eight for the fourth.

articles.body:
OpenAI ha rilasciato un nuovo modello di intelligenza artificiale sviluppato per individuare vulnerabilità critiche nei sistemi aziendali connessi. Si tratta di Gpt-6 Cyber, progettato per l'analisi avanzata del codice sorgente, l'individuazione di falle e la verifica delle correzioni da applicare agli ambienti esaminati. La tecnologia, resa accessibile a un ristretto numero di organizzazioni e ricercatori, è già stata utilizzata dall'azienda per scansionare il codice di Linux, consentendo di rintracciare 948 potenziali criticità, tra cui 588 anomalie precedentemente non documentate.

Linux costituisce il cuore-software non solo di server e data center, ma anche di molte infrastrutture che supervisionano le celle frigorifere nella logistica alimentare e farmaceutica. Il rilascio del modello si ricollega all'investimento da un miliardo di dollari annunciato a settembre da OpenAI a favore delle infrastrutture critiche, come reti elettriche e acquedotti, con l'obiettivo di rafforzare la difesa cyber prima che i criminali informatici sfruttino le vulnerabilità.

In questa direzione, la società di San Francisco ha pianificato alcune attività congiunte con ricercatori indipendenti ed esperti di sicurezza esterni per sottoporre a verifica preventiva la tenuta dei propri sistemi attraverso l'impiego diretto dei modelli. Stando allo sviluppatore, su un test che misura la capacità dei modelli di sfruttare una vulnerabilità specifica, Gpt-6 Cyber ha ottenuto un punteggio di 48,5%, in crescita rispetto al 32,1% registrato dal modello precedente. L'aggiornamento ha inoltre evitato di sfruttare servizi al di fuori del perimetro autorizzato nel 99,93% dei casi, in aumento rispetto al 94,49% di Gpt-5.6 Cyber.

articles.body:
A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports.

The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo — supposedly based on U.S. intelligence — also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.

A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. At the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.

The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

articles.title: Italian foreign minister says hackers leaked his personal data
articles.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has blamed pro-Russian hackers for publishing the details online.
articles.preview: Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says he has been targeted by "cyber-criminals" who published his personal data online because of his country's support for Ukraine. "For days now, cyber-criminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," Tajani wrote on X. He did not specify the nature of the threats, but said the hackers were also targeting his family.
articles.body:
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says he has been targeted by "cyber-criminals" who published his personal data online because of his country's support for Ukraine.

"For days now, cyber-criminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," Tajani wrote on X.

He did not specify the nature of the threats, but said the hackers were also targeting his family.

The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that is not indexed by common search engines and can only be accessed with specialist software.

"Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," Tajani said.

"Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities."

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed the incident on pro-Russian hackers and offered Tajani her "full solidarity".

"The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," she said in a statement.

Moscow has not publicly responded to the allegations.

Meloni also expressed concern about "circulation of false images" which she said were shared by members of Italy's opposition. She did not give details about the content of the images.

The Italian government has provided humanitarian and military support to Ukraine in its war against Russia.

Tajani, who is also the deputy prime minister, said the government was taking the threats seriously.

The government has selected 28 priority products and technologies, including semiconductors and artificial intelligence, for public and private investments totaling over ¥370 trillion, which are a pillar of its growth strategy, sources said Friday.

“Large-scale and strategic investment support measures are essential for establishing a domestic semiconductor supply chain,” Takaichi said at the meeting.

The 28 priority items were picked from 62 products and technologies in 17 strategic fields. They are expected to have significant economic spillover effects.

The government will formulate an implementation plan by the end of the year, designating the next five years as a period for intensive investments.

The priority items include vertical and physical AI, data centers, biopharmaceuticals, quantum computing, shipbuilding, and the refining of critical minerals.

In un anno le startup e le Pmi innovative in Sicilia sono passate da 725 a 794. L’aumento del 9,5%, rilevato dai dati diffusi da UniCredit alla Start Cup Sicilia 2026, coincide con l’avvio di una rete di poli finanziati dalla Regione con il Fesr 2021–2027. Intanto, alcune imprese tecnologiche raccolgono capitali, si aggregano e si aprono a nuovi mercati. La questione è se questi movimenti riescano a sostenersi a vicenda e a dare continuità al percorso che porta dalla ricerca ai primi clienti, dagli investimenti alle assunzioni.

Fondi Ue, 9,5 milioni per sedici poli

La mappa dell’intervento pubblico emerge dalla ricognizione di Maria Pia Bottino, dirigente responsabile dell’Unità tecnica di coordinamento della strategia regionale dell’innovazione del Dipartimento delle Attività produttive che ha curato il bando. Il programma Open Innovation Sicilia finanziato con Fondi Ue destina 9,5 milioni a sedici poli. Quindici offrono percorsi di accelerazione e sei di incubazione, con cinque strutture che svolgono entrambe le attività. Sette hanno sede nel Catanese, tre nel Palermitano, due nel Messinese, due nel Ragusano e uno nel Trapanese. Un altro opera tra Palermo e Messina.

Dal Premio all’Innovation Week

Su come collegare queste iniziative si concentra anche il lavoro della Fondazione Innovation Island. Nelle prime tre edizioni il Premio Innovazione Sicilia ha raccolto oltre 640 candidature. Con l’Innovation Week, dal 17 al 20 novembre tra Palermo e Catania, la Fondazione allarga quel percorso al confronto tra imprese, università e investitori. «Il nostro obiettivo – dice il presidente Biagio Semilia – è quello di accorciare le distanze nella mappa dell’ecosistema dell’innovazione che è già emersa in questi tre anni. A questa esigenza risponde l’Innovation Week e perseguono questo obiettivo anche le altre iniziative che abbiamo in campo nei prossimi mesi».

Le sperimentazioni nelle filiere produttive

La rete regionale si misura anzitutto con le esigenze delle filiere. A Partanna, nel Trapanese, INN-SO punta ad accompagnare almeno quindici imprese del vino, dell’olio e del lattiero-caseario, con circa 306 mila euro di aiuti alle aziende. A Ragusa, ELIS ed Eni prevedono prove di fattibilità nella chimica sostenibile e nel riciclo. A Palermo il programma SiLIFE è dedicato alle applicazioni dell’analisi dei dati nelle scienze della vita.

A questi interventi si affianca l’Innovation Hub di Meccatronica Cluster Sicilia, che aprirà il 10 novembre a Termini Imerese grazie a un investimento di 1,5 milioni finanziato dall’assessorato regionale alle Attività produttive. Le imprese, anche piccole, potranno accedere a robotica, intelligenza artificiale, macchinari e competenze specialistiche, condividendo i costi dell’innovazione. Un’Academy curerà la formazione delle figure richieste dalle fabbriche intelligenti. L’apertura sarà anche un’occasione di confronto con i competence center Bi-Rex e Meditech e il Polo Innovativo di Brescia, mentre un protocollo con il Distretto pugliese dell’industria culturale e digitale allargherà le collaborazioni fuori dall’Isola.

Due nuove Dmo, del Tigullio e della Spezia, si aggiungeranno alle tre già esistenti Sono cresciute le presenze turistiche in Liguria nei primi nove mesi dell’anno (18,6 milioni, pari a +3,16%) mentre la Regione ha avviato 10 milioni di euro d’investimenti, nel 2026, per il turismo e si prepara far crescere da tre a cinque le Dmo (Destination management organization) presenti sul territorio: in arrivo quelle di Tigullio e della Spezia.
articles.body:
Numeri in crescita nei primi nove mesi del 2026. Due nuove Dmo, del Tigullio e della Spezia, si aggiungeranno alle tre già esistenti

Sono cresciute le presenze turistiche in Liguria nei primi nove mesi dell’anno (18,6 milioni, pari a +3,16%) mentre la Regione ha avviato 10 milioni di euro d’investimenti, nel 2026, per il turismo e si prepara far crescere da tre a cinque le Dmo (Destination management organization) presenti sul territorio: in arrivo quelle di Tigullio e della Spezia. A spiegare la strategia per il settore, messa in moto dall’ente, è l’assessore regionale Luca Lombardi.

«Le risorse destinate al turismo nel 2026, per oltre 10 milioni di euro, comprendono - sottolinea - finanziamenti regionali e nazionali e si distribuiscono su diversi settori strategici: promozione turistica, marketing territoriale, valorizzazione delle identità locali, digitalizzazione, sviluppo delle destinazioni e sostegno agli eventi. Una parte degli investimenti è dedicata alla promozione della Liguria sui mercati nazionali e internazionali, mentre altre risorse sostengono le Pro loco, gli Eventi autentici liguri e le iniziative natalizie dei Comuni».

Fondi per eventi locali e Natale

In particolare, alle identità locali sono destinati 580 milioni: «250mila euro per 102 Eventi utentici, promossi dalle Pro Loco e 330mila euro per 77 manifestazioni organizzate dai Comuni, di cui 250mila di risorse regionali e 80mila di fondi ministeriali. Sono iniziative che raccontano le tradizioni, la cultura, l’enogastronomia e le caratteristiche dei nostri territori». Per il Natale, invece, «abbiamo messo a disposizione un bando per 460mila euro di contributi regionali, coinvolgendo 160 Comuni nelle quattro province. Un dato significativo è il valore complessivo dei progetti presentati, pari a circa 3,8 milioni, che dimostra la capacità delle amministrazioni locali di mobilitare ulteriori risorse e realizzare iniziative diffuse sul territori».

Con una parte dei 10 milioni si investe anche, prosegue l’assessore, «nel nuovo ecosistema digitale del turismo, nel rafforzamento dell’agenzia Inliguria e nell’avvio delle Dmo, per favorire una gestione sempre più coordinata delle destinazioni e la collaborazione tra pubblico e privato. A questi interventi si affianca il Patto per il lavoro nel turismo, per sostenere l’occupazione e favorire una maggiore continuità lavorativa nel settore. Particolare attenzione è rivolta anche al turismo outdoor, all’accessibilità e ai progetti di sviluppo del territorio. L’obiettivo è costruire un’offerta turistica sempre più competitiva, sostenibile e capace di attrarre visitatori durante tutto l’anno».

Cresce il sistema delle Destination management organization

Per quanto attiene alle Dmo (organismi che in liguria si basano su un modello di governance pubblico-privato che mette insieme Comuni, Cciaa e associazioni di categoria del turismo), le tre esistenti, cioè quelle di Imperia, Savona e Genova, «rappresentano - dice Lombardi - uno strumento fondamentale per costruire una governance turistica condivisa, mettendo in rete amministrazioni pubbliche, operatori economici e realtà territoriali. E ora sono in fase di formazione altre due Dmo: quella del Tigullio e quella della Spezia».

articles.title: 'Feeling guilty': Price hikes a tough sell in Japan despite inflation
articles.summary: The angst faced by Uniqlo and Saizeriya when they attempted to raise prices highlights the struggle Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country that has experienced decades of deflation.
articles.preview: The angst faced by Uniqlo and Saizeriya when they attempted to raise prices highlights the struggle Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country that has experienced decades of deflation. TOKYO: When Japan's "symbol of affordability" Uniqlo decided to increase the price of its basic socks last month, it sparked a backlash before the clothing titan made an immediate U-turn.
articles.body:
The angst faced by Uniqlo and Saizeriya when they attempted to raise prices highlights the struggle Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country that has experienced decades of deflation.

TOKYO: When Japan's "symbol of affordability" Uniqlo decided to increase the price of its basic socks last month, it sparked a backlash before the clothing titan made an immediate U-turn.

That came after Italian-style family restaurant chain Saizeriya issued an almost grovelling apology as it decided to add 20 yen (US$0.13) to the price of its trademark Milanese Doria, lamenting its "lack of effort".

The very public angst - including in one of the world's most recognisable clothing brands - highlights the struggles Japanese firms face as they battle rising costs in a country where decades of deflation have nurtured a consumer class averse to higher prices.

The Bank of Japan last month declared its 2 per cent inflation target had been met, after 13 years of ultra-loose monetary policy.

Measures unveiled in 2013 by then-prime minister Shinzo Abe - and continued by successive governments - were supposed to end a spiral of deflation that had plagued Japan for decades since the mid-1990s.

However, it wasn't until 2022 - when the Ukraine war triggered a global energy shock - that inflation started flickering back to life in resource-poor Japan.

Then the US-Israel war on Iran saw Tehran choke off the strategic Strait of Hormuz, slashing crude exports from the Middle East and impacting global supply chains, in turn sending company costs soaring.

"SORRY FOR OUR CUSTOMERS"

While firms in most countries have been able to lift prices accordingly - albeit to expected anger - those in Japan have to battle an inherent view that hikes are taboo.

Businesses big and small have found themselves hard-pressed to plough ahead with drastic price hikes to avoid alienating customers.

Decisive increases can be more of a risk for smaller, countryside businesses whose survival often hinges on loyal patronage by regular clients.

Sachi, 68, a ramen shop owner in western Japan's Okayama region, has been holding off on raising prices despite snowballing costs.

"When I imagine myself suddenly announcing a 200-yen hike, for example, I cannot help but feel guilty and sorry for our customers who have supported us for years," Sachi, who only gave her first name, told AFP during a recent trip to Tokyo.

"So my thinking is, 'I would rather persevere myself'. I think lots of tiny businesses are like that, especially in rural areas."

Uniqlo's decision to row back on its sock price hike came as it sought to protect its status as a paragon of affordability portrayed in local media.

Saizeriya, whose price increases went far beyond Doria to cover almost all menu items, issued a statement some saw as self-flagellating.

The company's president even vowed at a news conference to "look for any excuses to lower prices again", to the amazement of social media users.

Still, the chain kept other items such as wine - a stunningly cheap 100 yen per glass - unchanged because "we want it to be enjoyed casually", its public relations office told AFP.

"INSANELY HIGH"

Soaring grocery bills have left Japanese households less room to spend on other purchases, from dining out to clothing, even as these businesses grapple with rising labour and material costs of their own.

This is despite recent labour ministry statistics showing real wages in Japan have increased year-on-year for eight consecutive months.

"Food prices are getting insanely high, so I have to increasingly rely on stuff imported from overseas, because homegrown products cost me more," Tokyo office worker Kazuhiko Sato told AFP.

"I'm also eating out less," he said.

To make matters worse, the Bank of Japan has embarked on a period of interest rate increases to battle inflation, with borrowing costs at a more than 30-year high and likely to go up again.

Tsutomu Watanabe, the professor at the University of Tokyo's graduate school of economics, said: "Pay raises are still largely insufficient and not benefiting everyone."

A similar or even higher rate of inflation permeates other Group of Seven economies, but "wage hikes there have been decent enough to keep spending from weakening", he told AFP.

Therein lies a key difference from Japan, which essentially remains "a convalescent trying to recover from decades of deflation", the economist said.

"The pricing power of companies is still pretty much dictated by consumers" in Japan, he said.

He thinks it will be "another three to four years" before Japanese consumers undergo a mentality shift to accept chronic inflation as the natural result of steep wage increases.

"After 30 years of deflation, transitioning to a different regime inevitably takes some time," he said.

Gli aumenti delle bollette energetiche continuano a colpire duramente le imprese del terziario, con effetti sempre più pesanti sui costi di gestione e sulla competitività. A lanciare l’allarme è Confcommercio: secondo le stime dell’Osservatorio Energia della confederazione (OCEN), nel terzo trimestre del 2026 la spesa per elettricità e gas sostenuta dalle attività economiche del settore ha subito un’impennata a causa dei rincari delle quotazioni energetiche internazionali.

La spesa per l’elettricità

Nel terzo trimestre del 2026 - come denuncia l’OCEN - la spesa per l’elettricità a carico delle attività del settore è aumentata del 46,2% rispetto allo stesso periodo dello scorso anno e del 66,4% sul trimestre precedente, raggiungendo la cifra totale di 3,8 miliardi di euro.

La conseguenza è stato un evidente rincaro sulla bolletta media mensile, che ha sfiorato, complessivamente, i 29.700 euro. Sono stati colpiti in modo particolarmente duro bar (+133%), alberghi (+68%) e grandi superfici di vendita (+67%).

Il costo del gas

Anche sul fronte del gas Confcommercio rileva una situazione di forte criticità, con aumenti record: nel terzo trimestre la spesa complessiva delle imprese del terziario si è attestata a 788 milioni di euro, il 72,7% rispetto al 2025. La bolletta media mensile, invece, ha superato gli 11mila euro, per un aumento complessivo del 66,9% su base annua.

La ragione degli aumenti

A monte delle bollette sempre più salate, secondo Confcommercio, ci sarebbe la nuova impennata dei prezzi dell’energia sui mercati globali, che a inizio novembre hanno raggiunto i massimi dell’anno. Il petrolio Brent ha superato i 100 dollari al barile, registrando un aumento tendenziale del 69,4% a ottobre, mentre il gas al TTF di Amsterdam è salito a 96,3 euro/MWh (+173,4% su base annua).

articles.body:
Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.

“Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said. “Whether we could stay in that equilibrium for a very long time to come, we still don’t know.”

The remarks come a week after the BOJ marked a milestone by declaring that underlying inflation had reached the bank’s 2% target for the first time since the goal was introduced in 2013. Ueda didn’t offer any specific guidance on the central bank’s appetite to raise interest rates further, in an exchange with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.
